title: KV cache eviction & prefix-reuse deep dive with Atlas Data Systems
summary: Deep technical session to troubleshoot KV cache eviction and prefix reuse behavior seen by Atlas in long-context workloads. Covered paging, eviction policies, batching interactions, quantization tradeoffs, and on-prem/VPC placement impact. Agreed to run targeted eviction benchmark and share profiling artifacts and updated docs.
action_items: Priya Nambiar: provide eviction benchmark script + example config (due 2026-04-02)
Michael Rivera: share representative long-context prompt set and traffic distribution (due 2026-04-01)
Alex Chen: schedule on-prem perf run and book follow-up check-in (due 2026-04-06)
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-28
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 52 min
Recording: yes (auto)

Attendees:
- Alex Chen (Redwood AE)
- Priya Nambiar (Redwood SE)
- Michael Rivera (Atlas CTO)
- Sana Iqbal (Atlas Infra Lead)
- Robert Lee (Atlas ML Engineer)

Auto-summary (auto-generated): Atlas running long-context financial summarization workload sees KV cache thrash when sessions exceed ~64k tokens; prefix reuse inconsistent across similar sessions; paging to disk causing latency spikes. Looking for config and architectural fixes plus test harness.

Transcript:
[00:00] Alex Chen: hey everyone thanks for joining on time, um we'll go over the kv cache behavior you reported. Priya and I will lead, and then we can go deep into metrics and config. Michael, could you give the short repro context?
[00:22] Michael Rivera: sure, yeah thanks. So we run a summarization pipeline, long conversations with customers, typical session length 30k to 120k tokens. We started seeing latency spikes and some generation stalls around 50k plus, and the logs show a lot of cache evict events, sometimes repeated for the same prefix.
[00:38] Priya Nambiar: when you say evict events do you mean the runtime is explicitly evicting kv segments or are you seeing page faults / disk spill?
[00:46] Robert Lee: both. The monitoring shows evict markers, but then paging to NVMe and occasional backlog processing. We also noticed that when two sessions share a common prefix 6like the same onboarding preamble 7the cache reuse is intermittent; sometimes the second session hits, sometimes it misses.
[01:10] Sana Iqbal: and just to add, we're running Redwood Private in our VPC with dedicated nodes, 8xA10G, with quantized 4-bit model. We've tried raising mem limits on the pods but the eviction still happens under heavy concurrency.
[01:27] Priya Nambiar: good detail. A few quick clarifying q's: are you using persistent KV on disk (paging) enabled or relying purely on in-memory cache?
[01:35] Michael Rivera: we enabled paging because our average context is long; otherwise we'd OOM. But we expected smarter eviction / prefix reuse heuristics.
[01:43] Alex Chen: okay. So the three main areas we'll look at: 1) eviction policy and threshold tuning; 2) how paging interacts with batching and long-context workloads; 3) prefix keying and hash collisions or normalization that can prevent reuse.
[02:00] Priya Nambiar: right. I'll share the component diagram in chat  K V cache sits between tokenized prefix and runtime, we maintain per-session kv pointers and a global LRU-like segment store. If paging is enabled the least-recently-used segments are flushed to disk and rehydrated on demand which is the expensive path.
[02:22] Robert Lee: are there known heuristics to keep hot prefixes pinned? like an application-level pin?
[02:28] Priya Nambiar: yes, Redwood has a hot-pin option in Dedicated/Private configs; it's called prefix_pinning in the config. By default we are conservative because pinning increases memory pressure. For your workload a selective pin of common onboarding prefixes could reduce rehydration.
[02:44] Michael Rivera: is prefix_pinning safe with quantized models? we are running 4-bit and saw slightly higher CPU when pinning.
[02:52] Priya Nambiar: quantization mainly affects model memory and compute, but pinning affects kv memory. The CPU increase might come from serialization/deserialization of pinned segments to keep them coherent across nodes. We'll profile that.
[03:08] Sana Iqbal: we also see prefix reuse not happening when we redeploy  6 same prompt, different session id. Is there a session scoping rule?
[03:16] Alex Chen: yes by default some keys include session id and request-id metadata to avoid cross-tenant leaks. There is a normalize_prefix flag that strips volatile metadata for keying to improve reuse, but that has safety implications.
[03:29] Robert Lee: could that explain the intermittent hits? maybe normalization toggles on if we route to different nodes?
[03:37] Priya Nambiar: possibly. Also routing and shard affinity matters 7if the session lands on a node that doesn't have the segment in memory and it's been paged out, you'll miss the reuse. Smart routing with affinity is an option in your config.
[03:52] Michael Rivera: we're using round-robin for low latency, we didn't enable sticky routing. Would sticky/affinity cause CPU hot spots?
[04:00] Priya Nambiar: it can concentrate load but reduces cross-node evictions. There's a tradeoff: latency vs global memory efficiency. With dedicated nodes you can tune for affinity and scale horizontally.
[04:15] Alex Chen: quick sidebar: sometimes customers see evictions due to ephemeral KV fragmentation  7 lots of small segments cause the allocator to free larger contiguous blocks and trigger evict heuristics. Priya, maybe we show the fragmentation metric?
[04:28] Priya Nambiar: yes fragmentation metrics are in the perf dashboard  7 I'll point to the KV segment histograms.
[04:34] Robert Lee: we do see a lot of 1-4 token segments from turn-taking in chats, is there a coalescing option?
[04:41] Priya Nambiar: there's a defragmentation pass and an optional segment coalescer that merges small segments into a larger contiguous segment at checkpoints. It reduces overhead but adds CPU at checkpoint time.
[04:55] Alex Chen: let's talk about eviction thresholds  7 what are you set to?
[04:59] Michael Rivera: default; we didn't tune it.
[05:02] Priya Nambiar: defaults are tuned for general workloads; for long-context heavy customers we recommend increasing the in-memory threshold and enabling prefix_pinning for known hot prefixes. But that may require more RAM or forcing more aggressive paging policies to NVMe.
[05:17] Alex Chen: question: you mentioned NVMe paging causing latency spikes  7 are the spikes aligned with rehydration or with checkpoint flushes?
[05:25] Robert Lee: mostly rehydration on a cold hit, we see 200-800ms stalls occasionally, sometimes more under concurrency.
[05:33] Priya Nambiar: ok that aligns. Two mitigation paths: async rehydration (serve best-effort while fetching kv in background) or prefetching based on predicted reuse. Prefetch has some risk but for deterministic prefixes it's useful.
[05:47] Michael Rivera: is async rehydration in Redwood runtime? we've seen a "best-effort" fallback to generative mode but it causes coherence problems.
[05:56] Priya Nambiar: we have an async path that can synthesize an approximation while fetching exact kv; it's opt-in since it affects determinism. For your case we can test it on a dev cluster.
[06:06] Sana Iqbal: can we get the list of config fields to try? and what observability to pull?
[06:11] Alex Chen: yes we'll send a config matrix; Priya will include the perf metrics to check: eviction rate, rehydration latency histogram, segment size histogram, fragmentation ratio, node affinity misses, and paging throughput.
[06:23] Priya Nambiar: also include per-batch token distribution  7 batching behavior affects kv pressure. If a large batch forces many sessions to rehydrate at once, you get spikes.
[06:33] Robert Lee: on batching: we batch at app layer for throughput, could that be triggering eviction storms?
[06:39] Priya Nambiar: yes if many requests cause simultaneous cache reads for different prefixes, you'll have concurrent rehydrations. Staggering or jittering requests and smarter batching windows helps. There's an option in Redwood Optimize to suggest batching configs per workload.
[06:53] Michael Rivera: another oddity: seemingly identical prefixes sometimes get different hash keys  7 could encoding/tokenization differences cause this?
[07:01] Priya Nambiar: yes tokenization differences (like whitespace vs normalized unicode) can change keys. We recommend canonicalizing prompts at client side or enabling server-side normalization. We'll send a recommended sanitizer.
[07:15] Alex Chen: let's cover quantization: at 4-bit we saw memory shrink but sometimes KV serialization format differs. Are you using model sharded across GPUs?
[07:24] Robert Lee: yes model sharded across 4 GPUs per node.
[07:28] Priya Nambiar: okay sharding can increase the number of kv segments because each shard keeps its own cache pointers in some architectures. That increases metadata and can exacerbate eviction; quantization compacts model params but not necessarily KV metadata.
[07:42] Sana Iqbal: any best practice for on-prem vs hosted in this context?
[07:48] Priya Nambiar: hosted Redwood API can offload paging and we have cluster-level optimizations, but enterprise data policies pushed you to Private, which is fine. With Private we recommend dedicated NVMe per node with high IOPS and increasing in-memory thresholds, or using a hybrid approach: keep the hottest prefixes in a managed Redis-like hot store.
[08:06] Alex Chen: note also that network latency within a VPC can matter if you're using remote storage; local NVMe is preferred.
[08:12] Michael Rivera: good point. We currently mount a remote EBS-like volume  7 maybe that's the culprit.
[08:19] Robert Lee: yeah the IO tail latencies correlate with generation stalls.
[08:24] Priya Nambiar: moving to local NVMe for paging or using an in-node reserved partition helps. We'll propose config options.
[08:33] Alex Chen: quick pause  7 any security or compliance concerns about prefix normalization or pinning? we need to ensure no PII leakage across sessions.
[08:41] Michael Rivera: yes must preserve tenant isolation, SOC2 controls, and audit logs.
[08:46] Priya Nambiar: prefix normalization has a safe mode where we only strip volatile request headers and keep tenant id as part of the key. Pinning respects tenant boundaries. We'll provide documentation on audit and KMS for encryption at rest of paged segments.
[09:00] Robert Lee: do you have benchmarks showing pinning improves latency for reuse patterns?
[09:05] Priya Nambiar: we have internal perf tests; I'll attach a small set of results and the harness. For atlas's workload we'd like to run your prompt set to verify.
[09:15] Alex Chen: ok next let's dig into a specific repro Michael sent  7 the session trace shows repeated evict/rehydrate cycles for the same prefix every ~7 minutes. Any ideas?
[09:27] Priya Nambiar: that pattern often means the segment gets aged out by LRU windows because of a global threshold or because another background job allocates large chunks forcing eviction. Do you run overnight batch jobs?
[09:37] Michael Rivera: yes nightly retrain/ingest pipelines hit the same nodes briefly. Could that cause eviction of hot prefixes used in day-time sessions?
[09:44] Priya Nambiar: absolutely. We recommend namespace isolation or reserving a hot segment pool for real-time traffic.
[09:52] Robert Lee: is that doable in Private?
[09:55] Priya Nambiar: yes, you can configure reserved pools per tenant or route real-time traffic to nodes with reserved memory. We'll share the config snippet.
[10:05] Alex Chen: switching to prefix reuse keying  7 we suspect normalization off and routing inconsistency are the main culprit. Priya, can you walk through how keys are constructed?
[10:15] Priya Nambiar: sure, simplified: key = model_id + shard_id + prefix_hash + optional_session_tag. The prefix_hash is computed on token ids; normalization happens pre-tokenization if enabled. If session_tag is present it prevents cross-session reuse.
[10:29] Michael Rivera: so removing session_tag should allow reuse, but then risks cross-session leakage?
[10:34] Priya Nambiar: correct. We typically keep tenant_id and remove ephemeral session markers. That balances reuse and isolation.
[10:41] Robert Lee: could load-balancer-level hashing ensure same prefix routes to same node always?
[10:47] Priya Nambiar: yes sticky routing keyed on tenant_id+prefix_hash is an option; combine with pinning and affinity to minimize misses.
[10:56] Alex Chen: let's plan an experiment: 1) enable normalization, 2) enable pinning for top 10 prefixes, 3) enable sticky routing for those prefixes, and 4) run a synthetic load with your prompt set. Priya will provide a script.
[11:12] Michael Rivera: that sounds great. How do we measure success?
[11:16] Priya Nambiar: reduction in rehydration rate, lower 95/99 latency for generations, lower eviction rate per minute, and reduced paging throughput. We'll supply dashboards queries.
[11:27] Robert Lee: can we also test async rehydration as a fallback to see latency improvement?
[11:31] Priya Nambiar: yes we'll include it as a toggle in the harness. It's less deterministic but good for tail latency.
[11:39] Alex Chen: switching topic  7 prefix reuse with similar but not identical prompts: our fuzzy match cache suggestion?
[11:45] Priya Nambiar: Redwood has a prefix-similarity hint layer that allows approximate reuse using a short sketch of the prefix. It's experimental but may improve reuse for paraphrases. We'll discuss tradeoffs.
[11:57] Michael Rivera: interesting. Is that safe under compliance?
[12:01] Priya Nambiar: sketches don't keep full prompt, but we'd need to review with security. It can be opt-in and audited.
[12:09] Sana Iqbal: for on-prem concerns: how does KMS integrate for paged segment encryption?
[12:14] Priya Nambiar: we support customer-managed keys (KMIP/KMS/HSM) for encrypting NVMe pages and audit logs for decryption operations. We'll provide the integration doc.
[12:25] Alex Chen: good. Now a couple quick debug asks from Priya for the team: capture a heap dump around an eviction spike, the per-node eviction log, and the batch windows during the spike.
[12:37] Robert Lee: we can do that; what's the overhead?
[12:40] Priya Nambiar: small  7 heap dumps are transient and we recommend off-peak but for repro you can do it during a scheduled window. We'll provide exact commands.
[12:48] Michael Rivera: about metrics  7 how fine-grained are the eviction logs?
[12:51] Priya Nambiar: we log segment id, size, owner tenant, and timestamp. We'll point you to the parsing tool.
[12:58] Alex Chen: competitor note  7 several customers compared this to CloudCo AI's managed endpoints; CloudCo does not expose on-prem pinning so it's a differentiator for Redwood in Private mode.
[13:08] Sana Iqbal: interesting. We also looked at InferX but their quantization flow was different.
[13:14] Priya Nambiar: thanks for mentioning  7 those are useful data points.
[13:19] Alex Chen: ok wrapping toward next steps and responsibilities  7 Priya?
[13:23] Priya Nambiar: we'll deliver: 1) eviction benchmark harness + runbook, 2) config matrix for normalization/pinning/affinity, 3) perf dashboard queries, 4) small script for async rehydration toggle. Expect those in the next 3-5 business days.
[13:38] Michael Rivera: we'll send the prompt set and a sampling of logs by Friday.
[13:43] Alex Chen: we'll also propose an on-prem perf slot to run the harness with you and collect heap dumps. I'll coordinate calendars.
[13:51] Robert Lee: one last question  7 any quick wins we can flip today?
[13:55] Priya Nambiar: enable normalization at server-side in safe mode (no session strip), and increase in-memory kv threshold by 15%  7 both are low-risk and reversible.
[14:05] Sana Iqbal: we'll try that and let you know if anything pops.
[14:09] Alex Chen: great. Thanks all  7 we'll follow up with the artifacts.

[14:20] (end of recorded detailed discussion; remaining minutes used for scheduling and brief wrap)
[14:45] Alex Chen: scheduling note  7 follow-up check-in in one week to review benchmark results.
[15:00] Michael Rivera: thanks everyone.
